lines: Here's a real pipeline whose own middle stage only ever hands a batch forward through a channel that holds a small, fixed number of them at once.
The stage at the far end is deliberately slow. Does memory keep piling up while the fast end waits on the slow one, or does something hold it back?
answer: Once that small channel fills up, the fast end simply has to wait its turn.

lines: Run it for real: across an entire real run of many batches against that same slow ending, the most memory this pipeline ever holds at once stays small, just a handful of batches worth.
Now swap in a version whose channels have no real limit at all, and whose own stages each make a fresh copy of a batch before handing it onward.
Same fast beginning, same slow ending underneath it. Does its own peak memory land anywhere close to the first version?
answer: With nothing to push back against, the fast end just keeps going, piling up copies the slow end hasn't gotten to yet.

lines: Run it for real: that second pipeline's own peak memory climbs to nearly the entire run's worth of bytes, because its fast end never once had a reason to pause.
steps.takeaway: A channel with no real limit removes the one signal that would have told a fast producer to slow down.

lines: Put those two real peaks side by side, from the identical workload, the identical slow ending underneath both.
Is that gap between them a small, incidental thing, or something sturdier than that?
answer: It's a real, structural gap, many times over, that holds for as long as the fast end keeps outrunning the slow one.

lines: Run it for real: the pipeline with no real limit peaks at several times what the bounded one ever reaches, for the identical workload and the identical slow ending.
steps.takeaway: A bounded channel's own real limit is what turns a fast producer's head start into backpressure, not goodwill.

lines: One real, well-known piece of documentation describes exactly this, in its own words.
A channel that's actually full rejects the next handoff until room opens back up. A channel with no real limit always accepts the handoff right away, with nothing behind it to ever say no.
steps.takeaway: A buffer handed forward through a channel that can say no keeps memory bounded; copying into one that cannot does not.

lines: So here's what both of these real runs were really showing: moving a batch forward through a channel that can genuinely refuse it keeps a pipeline's own memory in check, no matter how far behind the slow end falls.
Copying that same batch into a channel that never refuses anything removes the only thing standing between a fast beginning and a pile of memory nobody asked for.
Either way, it's the identical real lesson: a limit that's only ever assumed isn't a limit at all, until something downstream can actually enforce it.
